story.title: ADAEZE'S ORCHARD
story.deck: A flood canal that would keep twenty thousand people dry has to cross the one hillside Illuminara's mother will not give up, and the rains are twenty-one weeks away. Her mother will not say why. Illuminara has to learn what a refusal is carrying, and whether anyone's explanation of it is right.
story.shape: Five scenes across five months: a refusal that explains nothing, a walk in which the hill's weight runs in a straight line, a wager with three rival explanations and one natural experiment, a three-hour storm test whose needle decides between them, and the first night of the rains.

scenes.title: A Reasonable No
paragraphs: *Okafor orchard, Kestrel Hill · Day One, 07:10*

The orchard smelled of guavas the pickers had missed, sweet and a little rotten, and Corinna Saleh had pinned her plans to the hood of the authority's truck so the wind could not read them. Below the lower wall the town of Marrow Ford lay in its river bend, twenty thousand people on ground that had flooded twice in living memory and would flood again in twenty-one weeks.

The diversion was easy to say. When the river crested, a canal across Kestrel Saddle would carry thirty-eight cubic metres a second into the old quarry for the six hours the crest lasted, and the lower town would keep its streets. The saddle's lowest line ran through the third terrace of Adaeze Okafor's orchard.

**Corinna Saleh**  
The north route misses you. So does the south. Fourteen months and sixteen. We have twenty-one weeks.
Adaeze came down between the rows with a basket on her hip, small and straight-backed, and read the plans the way a woman reads a bill.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
No.

**Corinna Saleh**  
The authority can compel, Mrs Okafor. It would rather not.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
Then compel. You will need a magistrate and a year. I have the year. Ask my daughter how much you have.

Illuminara had two alignments in her head that missed the orchard entirely, and she knew the price of each in months. She had come up the hill ready to argue. She found a wall instead, and her first thought was that walls like this are built out of grief and inheritance, four generations of both. She filed the refusal there. It was the first mistake.

**Illuminara**  
Mama. Why?

**Adaeze Okafor**  
You are making the face, Nara. The one that has already decided what I mean.

**Illuminara**  
Then tell me what you mean.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
Walk the hill with me. Not with her, and not with a clipboard. Wednesday, early. Wear shoes.
Corinna wrote the date on the back of her hand. Adaeze gave her a guava, and neither of them seemed to know what the other had won.

scenes.title: What the Hill Carries
paragraphs: *Okafor orchard, third terrace · Day Three, 06:00*

Illuminara had two ways of walking a hill. The ordinary one used her feet. The other let the slope's weight come up through her soles as a map: where the soil leaned on the clay, where the clay leaned on the stone, ten thousand tons settling downhill as quietly as a held breath, every load finding its road to the ground. It told her where force went. It never told her why.
Under the third terrace the weight did something it should not have done. It ran in a line.
She stopped between two trees. Adaeze, ahead of her with the basket, stopped without turning round.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
Found it.

**Illuminara**  
There is a seam under here. Forty metres, perfectly straight, four metres down. Rock does not do straight.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
My father said never cut across the third terrace. He never said why, and he was not a man you asked twice. I plant where his grandmother planted. The trees hold the hill, Nara. That is all I know and all I will swear to.

Illuminara knelt and put her palm on the wet grass. Roots go a metre down, perhaps a little more, and the seam lay four below that. She said so as gently as the fact allowed, and Adaeze took it the way she took weather.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
Then it is deeper, and my trees are still standing on it.
The next idea arrived whole, the way good ones do, and Illuminara liked it at once. The terraces already stepped down the hill like a staircase built for water.

**Illuminara**  
Line the lower three terraces and let the flood run down them. The cut never touches the third terrace. Every tree stays.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
No.

**Illuminara**  
You have not heard the numbers.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
A guava can stand three hours of wet feet. You are offering it six, on top of ground that has to drain afterwards, not hold. Those lower rows live because the water goes through this hill. You want to put the river on top of what my family sent underneath.

It was the second no, and it was not sentiment. Illuminara had been designing around the orchard as if it were a surface to be spared while the engineering happened somewhere else. Adaeze was telling her that the orchard was the engineering.

**Illuminara**  
Underneath where?

Adaeze led her up to a stone lid sunk in the grass above the third terrace, and then down, a long way down, to a hole the size of a fist in the lower wall, where a thread of water ticked onto a flat stone.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
The spring box. And that is the drip. My father's drain. Nobody has cleaned it since he died.

**Illuminara**  
Mama, that is the seam.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
That is a drain. A drain is a pipe for the trees' feet.

**Illuminara**  
A drain forty metres long, laid straight under the heaviest part of the hill, with the hill leaning on it. I do not think it is only for the trees.

scenes.title: Three Predictions
paragraphs: *Okafor orchard, sixth terrace · Day Five, 16:20*

Tomas Reyes unrolled sensor cable behind his truck like a man feeding out line to a very long, very patient animal. He was the authority's geotechnical engineer, a heavy, careful person who had spent a career being right about hills, and he was not offended by a sprinkler test. He was only unconvinced. Corinna stood by the tailgate with her arms folded and the date still faint on her hand.

Idowu Bello had walked over from the next plot with his hands in his pockets. He had cleared his half of the hillside in a dry year and sold it to the authority in the spring, and he looked at the bare slope the way a man looks at a decision.

**Idowu Bello**  
Use my ground. There is nothing on it to protect, and I would like to know whether I should be nervous.
Tomas wrote the predictions on the back of the authority's own form, so that no one could say later that they had been fitted to the result.

**Tomas Reyes**  
Mine first. This hill is fractured sandstone. Water leaves through the cracks wherever you put it, so the orchard, your father's drain and Idowu's bare ground will all behave alike. Three plots, one needle.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
Mine is shorter. Trees hold. The plots with trees stay quiet. Idowu's goes.

**Illuminara**  
Mine splits both of yours. The drain holds the hill. The plot on the drain line stays quiet. A plot with trees but no working drain goes with Idowu's ground.
Adaeze considered the slope, and Illuminara watched her decide to be generous.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
The sixth terrace, east corner. The inlet silted the year of the big wind. Water stands there every spring, and I have never got a good guava out of it.

**Illuminara**  
You could have told me that on Monday.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
You did not ask me a question on Monday. You told me a plan.
They settled the stakes without anyone raising a voice.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
If Tomas is right, I sign the saddle cut myself. If I am right, you find another road. If my daughter is right, she says so to my face, and then she cleans my drain.

**Corinna Saleh**  
One condition from me. If the drain line crosses ten, the saddle is dead and I take the south route, sixteen months, and I tell the town today that the rains will find it unprotected.

**Corinna Saleh**  
Every day on this is a day the rains do not give back.

**Illuminara**  
Four days. And Tomas has just written you a geotechnical report on the back of a form.

scenes.title: The Needle
paragraphs: *Okafor orchard, three plots · Day Nine, 13:05*

The sprinklers were set to the storm the hill sees once in a century. Tomas stood over his needle with a flask of tea. Illuminara tipped a cup of green dye into the spring box and put the lid back, and Adaeze carried a bucket down to the drip and sat on it with her hand flat on the wall.
At thirty-eight minutes a green thread came out of the hole in the stone. Adaeze looked at it for a while.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
A kettle and a half.

The needle on the drain line never passed six. The corner of the sixth terrace, with its trees standing in it, crossed ten at ninety-five minutes, which was where Tomas had said the hill stopped being sure of itself. Idowu's bare ground crossed it at eighty-five. At a hundred and five a painted stake on Idowu's slope moved four millimetres, and Tomas shut off the water with a flat hand, like a man stopping an orchestra.

**Tomas Reyes**  
The drain line was back to two forty minutes after the water stopped. The corner went over ten with the trees in it. Bedrock is out. Same sandstone under all three and they do not agree. I was wrong, and I am glad to be wrong in a way I can write down.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
My trees did not hold it.
Illuminara crouched beside her.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
Do not be kind. Be accurate.

**Illuminara**  
Your trees did not hold the hill. Your father's drain did, and your trees have been drinking from it for eighty years. That is why the fruit is good.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
That is kind and accurate. I will allow it.
Illuminara had drawn it in the truck cab on Day Seven, on the chance that she would be allowed to use it. She unrolled it on the bucket lid.

**Illuminara**  
I cannot cut the third terrace and I will not drown your rows. So the canal goes in the bottom seven metres of the orchard, along the wall, in precast panels. The drip comes out into it through a one-way flap. In flood the canal cannot push water back up your father's drain, and in dry months the drain runs out into the canal as it always has. Tomas clears the silted inlet in the sixth corner. Where the flood outgrows the quarry, a weir at the head of the canal puts the surplus back in the river below the town, where Corinna's survey says the channel can take it.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
Seven metres of what? How many trees?

**Illuminara**  
Nine trees stand in the strip. I can save two, and you choose which.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
Seven, then, and I choose the seven. If the flood ever needs more than the strip, you ask me, and if I say no, it is no.

**Illuminara**  
The design works on the strip alone. I made it so it would still work if you refused me everything else.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
Good. And I plant the bank. Nobody else touches a root.

**Corinna Saleh**  
The strip is not in the permit.

**Illuminara**  
Clause fourteen lets you vary the line by four hundred metres where the owner consents and a geotechnical report supports it. You have a consenting owner and a report on a form.

**Corinna Saleh**  
Seventeen weeks to build. You have nineteen.

**Illuminara**  
Two weeks of slack.

**Corinna Saleh**  
And rain does not read calendars.

scenes.title: The Drip
paragraphs: *Okafor orchard, new bank · Month Five, the first night of the rains*
The last panel went in eight days before the rain. Along the lower wall stood seven pale stumps that Adaeze had chosen herself, oldest first, and had not allowed anyone to photograph.

The river began to rise at 01:40. Corinna's voice came out of the control hut radio, flat and exact, and at 02:05 she said the gates were open. The canal filled with a sound like a long breath let out. At the foot of the wall the flap on the drip clapped shut once under the pressure, and the thread of water stopped.
Adaeze stood under an umbrella that was not helping and took her daughter's arm without looking, with the grip of a woman checking a rope. Below them, Marrow Ford kept its lights on.

**Corinna Saleh**  
Basin at half. Spill weir shut. Lower town is dry, every street.
Eight hundred and twenty thousand cubic metres went into the old quarry before the crest passed at a little after eight. It had room for eleven hundred thousand. The spill weir never opened.
When the canal began to drain, the flap lifted by itself. For a moment nothing happened, and then the stone under the wall began to tick.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
It's running.

In the grey light Adaeze knelt on the new bank with a tray of rooted cuttings she had taken from the oldest of the seven before it came down. Illuminara held the pot while she settled the first one in.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
Straight, Nara. You still do not call before you come.

**Illuminara**  
No.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
Good. Then I will keep the kettle on.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
Then compel. You will need a magistrate and a year. I have the year. Ask my daughter how much you have.

Illuminara had two alignments in her head that missed the orchard entirely, and she knew the price of each in months. She had come up the hill ready to argue. She found a wall instead, and her first thought was that walls like this are built out of grief and inheritance, four generations of both. She filed the refusal there. It was the first mistake.

**Illuminara**  
Mama. Why?

**Adaeze Okafor**  
You are making the face, Nara. The one that has already decided what I mean.

**Illuminara**  
Then tell me what you mean.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
Walk the hill with me. Not with her, and not with a clipboard. Wednesday, early. Wear shoes.
Corinna wrote the date on the back of her hand. Adaeze gave her a guava, and neither of them seemed to know what the other had won.

scenes.title: What the Hill Carries
paragraphs: *Okafor orchard, third terrace · Day Three, 06:00*

Illuminara had two ways of walking a hill. The ordinary one used her feet. The other let the slope's weight come up through her soles as a map: where the soil leaned on the clay, where the clay leaned on the stone, ten thousand tons settling downhill as quietly as a held breath, every load finding its road to the ground. It told her where force went. It never told her why.
Under the third terrace the weight did something it should not have done. It ran in a line.
She stopped between two trees. Adaeze, ahead of her with the basket, stopped without turning round.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
Found it.

**Illuminara**  
There is a seam under here. Forty metres, perfectly straight, four metres down. Rock does not do straight.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
My father said never cut across the third terrace. He never said why, and he was not a man you asked twice. I plant where his grandmother planted. The trees hold the hill, Nara. That is all I know and all I will swear to.

Illuminara knelt and put her palm on the wet grass. Roots go a metre down, perhaps a little more, and the seam lay four below that. She said so as gently as the fact allowed, and Adaeze took it the way she took weather.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
Then it is deeper, and my trees are still standing on it.
The next idea arrived whole, the way good ones do, and Illuminara liked it at once. The terraces already stepped down the hill like a staircase built for water.

**Illuminara**  
Line the lower three terraces and let the flood run down them. The cut never touches the third terrace. Every tree stays.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
No.

**Illuminara**  
You have not heard the numbers.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
A guava can stand three hours of wet feet. You are offering it six, on top of ground that has to drain afterwards, not hold. Those lower rows live because the water goes through this hill. You want to put the river on top of what my family sent underneath.

It was the second no, and it was not sentiment. Illuminara had been designing around the orchard as if it were a surface to be spared while the engineering happened somewhere else. Adaeze was telling her that the orchard was the engineering.

**Illuminara**  
Underneath where?

Adaeze led her up to a stone lid sunk in the grass above the third terrace, and then down, a long way down, to a hole the size of a fist in the lower wall, where a thread of water ticked onto a flat stone.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
The spring box. And that is the drip. My father's drain. Nobody has cleaned it since he died.

**Illuminara**  
Mama, that is the seam.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
That is a drain. A drain is a pipe for the trees' feet.

**Illuminara**  
A drain forty metres long, laid straight under the heaviest part of the hill, with the hill leaning on it. I do not think it is only for the trees.

scenes.title: Three Predictions
paragraphs: *Okafor orchard, sixth terrace · Day Five, 16:20*

Tomas Reyes unrolled sensor cable behind his truck like a man feeding out line to a very long, very patient animal. He was the authority's geotechnical engineer, a heavy, careful person who had spent a career being right about hills, and he was not offended by a sprinkler test. He was only unconvinced. Corinna stood by the tailgate with her arms folded and the date still faint on her hand.

Idowu Bello had walked over from the next plot with his hands in his pockets. He had cleared his half of the hillside in a dry year and sold it to the authority in the spring, and he looked at the bare slope the way a man looks at a decision.

**Idowu Bello**  
Use my ground. There is nothing on it to protect, and I would like to know whether I should be nervous.
Tomas wrote the predictions on the back of the authority's own form, so that no one could say later that they had been fitted to the result.

**Tomas Reyes**  
Mine first. This hill is fractured sandstone. Water leaves through the cracks wherever you put it, so the orchard, your father's drain and Idowu's bare ground will all behave alike. The needles read pore pressure in kilopascals, and my model says the slope moves at ten. On the drain plot I set a twin needle six metres off the line, same stone, same depth. If I am right, the twins read alike.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
Mine is shorter. Trees hold. The plots with trees stay quiet. Idowu's goes.

**Illuminara**  
Mine splits both of yours. The drain holds the hill. The needle on the drain line stays quiet, and its twin, six metres away in the same stone, does not. A plot with trees but no working drain goes with Idowu's ground.
Adaeze considered the slope, and Illuminara watched her decide to be generous.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
The sixth terrace, east corner. The inlet silted the year of the big wind. Water stands there every spring, and I have never got a good guava out of it.

**Illuminara**  
You could have told me that on Monday.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
You did not ask me a question on Monday. You told me a plan.
They settled the stakes without anyone raising a voice.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
If Tomas is right, I sign the saddle cut myself. If I am right, you find another road. If my daughter is right, she says so to my face, and then she cleans my drain.

**Corinna Saleh**  
One condition from me. If the drain line crosses ten, the saddle is dead and I take the south route, sixteen months, and I tell the town today that the rains will find it unprotected. And if a test pour leaves under half a metre of freeboard, I tell them that day too.

**Corinna Saleh**  
Every day on this is a day the rains do not give back.

**Illuminara**  
Four days. And Tomas has just written you a geotechnical report on the back of a form.

scenes.title: The Needle
paragraphs: *Okafor orchard, three plots · Day Nine, 13:05*

The sprinklers were set to the storm the hill sees once in a century. Tomas stood over his needle with a flask of tea. Illuminara tipped a cup of green dye into the spring box and put the lid back, and Adaeze carried a bucket down to the drip and sat on it with her hand flat on the wall.
At thirty-eight minutes a green thread came out of the hole in the stone. Adaeze looked at it for a while.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
A kettle and a half.

The needle on the drain line never passed six kilopascals. Its twin, six metres off the line in the same stone at the same depth, climbed past nine. The corner of the sixth terrace, with its trees standing in it, crossed ten at ninety-five minutes, which was where Tomas had said the hill stopped being sure of itself. Idowu's bare ground crossed it at eighty-five. At a hundred and five a painted stake on Idowu's slope moved four millimetres, and Tomas shut off the water with a flat hand, like a man stopping an orchestra.

**Tomas Reyes**  
The drain line was back to two forty minutes after the water stopped. Its twin was still above six. Fractured sandstone says those two match, and they do not. The corner went over ten with the trees in it. Bedrock is out. I was wrong, and I am glad to be wrong in a way I can write down.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
My trees did not hold it.
Illuminara crouched beside her.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
Do not be kind. Be accurate.

**Illuminara**  
Your trees did not hold the hill. Your father's drain did, and your trees have been drinking from it for eighty years. That is why the fruit is good.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
That is kind and accurate. I will allow it.
Illuminara had drawn it in the truck cab on Day Seven, on the chance that she would be allowed to use it. She unrolled it on the bucket lid.

**Illuminara**  
I cannot cut the third terrace and I will not drown your rows. So the canal goes in the bottom seven metres of the orchard, along the wall, in precast panels. The drip comes out into it through a one-way flap. In flood the canal cannot push water back up your father's drain, and in dry months the drain runs out into the canal as it always has. Tomas clears the silted inlet in the sixth corner. Where the flood outgrows the quarry, a weir at the head of the canal puts the surplus back in the river below the town.

**Tomas Reyes**  
Five metres of bed between concrete walls, two of water: ten square metres. Thirty-eight through ten is three point eight metres a second on a fall of one in four hundred. Panels take that. Soil would not, so no water touches the bank, and a metre of freeboard stands above the surface.

**Corinna Saleh**  
And past thirty-eight?

**Tomas Reyes**  
The weir hands it to the river below the town. That channel takes ten more before it tops its bank, and the worst flood in your survey peaks at forty-six.

**Corinna Saleh**  
Then the proof comes before the last panel, not after it. A test pour at thirty-eight for six hours, Tomas's gauge on the rim. If it leaves under half a metre of freeboard, the strip is dead, Mrs Okafor's orchard is untouched, I take the south route, and I tell the town that day.

**Tomas Reyes**  
It will not come near. I will stand at the gauge anyway.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
Seven metres of what? How many trees?

**Illuminara**  
Nine trees stand in the strip. I can save two, and you choose which.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
Seven, then, and I choose the seven. If the flood ever needs more than the strip, you ask me, and if I say no, it is no.

**Illuminara**  
The design works on the strip alone. I made it so it would still work if you refused me everything else.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
Good. And I plant the bank. Nobody else touches a root.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
Your flap is a door nobody can open. Every October my father poured the spring through the drain from the box above the third terrace and flushed it clean. Shut a flap on that and the silt stays in the pipe, and in five years you have my sixth-corner inlet, forty metres long.
Illuminara looked at the flap on her drawing. She had shown the water how to leave and had not shown anyone how to keep it leaving.

**Illuminara**  
A chain. The flap lifts on a chain run up a sleeve to a hatch in the bank, and the flush goes through when you pull it.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
When I pull it. In October. And nobody else touches the chain.
Illuminara redrew the flap in pencil on the bucket lid, with her mother's hand on the corner to keep the paper flat.

**Corinna Saleh**  
The strip is not in the permit.

**Illuminara**  
Clause fourteen lets you vary the line by four hundred metres where the owner consents and a geotechnical report supports it. You have a consenting owner and a report on a form.

**Corinna Saleh**  
Seventeen weeks to build. You have nineteen.

**Illuminara**  
Two weeks of slack.

**Corinna Saleh**  
And rain does not read calendars.

scenes.title: The Drip
paragraphs: *Okafor orchard, new bank · Month Five, the first night of the rains*

The last panel went in eight days before the rain. Along the lower wall stood seven pale stumps that Adaeze had chosen herself, oldest first, and had not allowed anyone to photograph. Tomas had run the test pour in month four, thirty-eight for six hours with his gauge on the rim, and the water had stood a metre and six centimetres below the lip. Corinna had signed the strip that afternoon.

The river began to rise at 01:40. Corinna's voice came out of the control hut radio, flat and exact, and at 02:05 she said the gates were open. The canal filled with a sound like a long breath let out. At the foot of the wall the flap on the drip clapped shut once under the pressure, and the thread of water stopped.
Adaeze stood under an umbrella that was not helping and took her daughter's arm without looking, with the grip of a woman checking a rope. Below them, Marrow Ford kept its lights on.

**Corinna Saleh**  
Basin at half. Spill weir shut. Lower town is dry, every street.
Eight hundred and twenty thousand cubic metres went into the old quarry before the crest passed at a little after eight. It had room for eleven hundred thousand. The spill weir never opened.

When the canal began to drain, the flap lifted by itself. For a moment nothing happened, and then the stone under the wall began to tick. A chain ran from the flap up its sleeve to a hatch in the new bank, and the first October flush was already in Adaeze's planting plan, in her own hand.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
It's running.

In the grey light Adaeze knelt on the new bank with a tray of rooted cuttings she had taken from the oldest of the seven before it came down. Illuminara held the pot while she settled the first one in.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
Straight, Nara. You still do not call before you come.

**Illuminara**  
No.

**Adaeze Okafor**  
Good. Then I will keep the kettle on.
